sources.title: TCP vs UDP: Differences Between TCP & UDP Protocols
What Is the Difference Between TCP and UDP?
TCP vs UDP | 10 Key Differences Explained with Table & Examples

points.point: TCP is connection-oriented and uses a 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) before data transfer.
UDP is connectionless — no handshake, no session state, packets are sent directly.
TCP guarantees delivery via acknowledgements (ACKs) and retransmission of lost segments.
UDP does not guarantee delivery; lost packets are simply dropped.
TCP maintains the order of segments using sequence numbers.
UDP does not preserve order; packets may arrive out of sequence.
TCP implements flow control using a sliding window to prevent overwhelming the receiver.
UDP has no flow control.
TCP implements congestion control (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, fast recovery).
UDP has no congestion control — the sender does not adapt to network conditions.
TCP header is 20 bytes minimum (up to 60 bytes with options).
UDP header is a fixed 8 bytes.
TCP is slower due to handshake, ACKs, and retransmission overhead.
UDP is faster and lighter because it has no setup or reliability overhead.
TCP performs error recovery via retransmission; UDP only performs a checksum and drops bad packets.
TCP supports unicast only; UDP supports unicast, multicast, and broadcast.
TCP is used by HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SSH, SMTP, IMAP, POP3 — applications where data integrity matters.
UDP is used by DNS, DHCP, NTP, SNMP, RTP (voice/video), QUIC — applications where speed matters.
Both TCP and UDP are Layer 4 (transport layer) protocols in the TCP/IP model.
TCP is defined in RFC 793; UDP is defined in RFC 768.
